svg.title: Night vision: dark adaptation and protection
svg.desc: Bars compare adaptation: the cones adapt rapidly, while the rods take approximately 30 minutes to fully adapt to darkness; a bright light can completely destroy night adaptation. Protect night vision with N-15 sunglasses, low flightdeck lighting, a dim white light flashlight, avoiding bright areas and airfield light discipline. Night vision is degraded by altitude above 4,000 feet without oxygen, smoking, drugs, exhaustion, alcohol, hunger and lack of vitamin A.
svg.text: Night vision: dark adaptation and protection
Once fully adapted to darkness, the rods are 10,000 times more sensitive to light than the cones,
making them the primary receptors for night vision.
Dark adaptation: how long the eyes take
Cones
Rods
adapt rapidly
take much longer: approximately 30 minutes to fully adapt to darkness
Dark begins
approximately 30 minutes
Leaving a bright room takes longer than leaving a dim one.
A bright light can completely destroy night adaptation.
Protect your night vision
Wear neutral density (N-15) sunglasses or
equivalent in bright sunlight before a night
flight; this increases the rate of dark adaptation
Keep flightdeck lighting as low as possible; after
reaching altitude, allow time to adjust (instrument
lights and outside references)
To read maps, charts and checklists, use a dim
white light flashlight and avoid shining it in
anyone's eyes
Turn away from high intensity lighting and fly in
the periphery of the lighted area; avoid direct
overflight of built-up, brightly lit areas
Airfield: lowest usable lighting, light discipline
with headlights and flashlights, park where the
least lighting exists, avoid approach and departure
routes over highways and residential areas
What degrades it
Altitude: without supplemental oxygen, night vision
declines measurably at pressure altitudes above
4,000 feet
At 12,000 feet at night, parts of normal vision may
be missing or unfocused; after a climb from 8,000
to 12,000 feet for 30 minutes, visual acuity may
not return for over an hour even after descending
to 8,000 feet
Smoking: smokers lose 20 percent of their night
vision at sea level, equal to a physiological
altitude of 5,000 feet
Drugs, exhaustion, poor physical conditioning,
alcohol (residual effects last)
Missed meals (low blood sugar) and a lack of
vitamin A (extra vitamin A does not increase night
vision)
